outcome: Nothing has settled whether every Fermat number is square-free, and no case of it has been settled since 26 January 2024: the Fermat-specific events since then are a 2026 Integers note that restates Jakóbczyk's 1951 hypothesis as open (full text not decoded), an unattributed 2026 partial-progress page that says it is not a proof, and new prime factors of composite Fermat numbers, which say nothing about square factors; no AI system is credited with any step on this question.
problem_asks: Whether every Fermat number F_n = 2^(2^n) + 1 (n = 0, 1, 2, ...) is square-free, i.e. whether there is no n and no prime p with p^2 dividing F_n. One universal claim: over all n >= 0 and all primes p. No separate parts. Wikipedia's January 2024 wording is 'Are all Fermat numbers square-free?'; the Wikipedia Fermat number article rephrases the same open question as 'Does a Fermat number exist that is not square-free?'.

events.what_happened: Leroy J. Warren and Henry Gilbert Bray, 'On the square-freeness of Fermat and Mersenne numbers', Pacific Journal of Mathematics 22(3), pp. 563-564. The note records that it has been conjectured that the Fermat and Mersenne numbers are all square-free, then proves a necessary condition: if some Fermat or Mersenne number is not square-free, then for any prime p whose square divides it, 2^(p-1) = 1 (mod p^2). It states that only two such primes were known, and that neither divides any Fermat or Mersenne number. I read the MSP abstract page only; the PDF could not be decoded.
events.revisions: None found. The date is the journal publication date; no earlier version was found.
events.delivers: A conditional reduction, not a resolution. It shows that any non-square-free Fermat number would have a square prime factor p satisfying the Wieferich congruence 2^(p-1) = 1 (mod p^2), and that neither of the two then-known Wieferich primes (1093 and 3511) divides any Fermat or Mersenne number. It does not show that any F_n is square-free, and does not show that any F_n is not.
events.remains: Everything except the reduction: whether any prime p with p^2 | F_n exists. The note excludes only the two then-known Wieferich primes as square divisors and leaves every other prime open.

checked_by.who: Pacific Journal of Mathematics referees (not named in the record I could read)
checked_by.qualification: Refereed journal of record for the paper
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted the note for publication (refereeing presumed; referee reports are not public)

events.time_since_posted: About 59 years. Later engagement found only as citation: the 2026 ProofAtlas page cites it.
events.directly_checkable: The necessary congruence is a finite check for any given candidate prime p: 2^(p-1) mod p^2.
events.direction: Partial and conditional. It constrains what a counterexample would have to look like (its square prime factor must be a Wieferich prime) and rules out the two known Wieferich primes as square divisors. It leans toward the expected answer (square-free) without deciding it.

events.what_happened: P. Ribenboim, 'On the square factors of the numbers of Fermat and Ferentinou-Nicolakopoulou', Mathematike Epitheorese (Μαθηματική Επιθεώρηση) 20 (1980), pp. 81-91, in Greek. I know it only from a bibliographic database record that surfaced in search. The same title appears with a 1979 Deltio (Δελτίο) citation and a 1988 Euklides (Ευκλείδης) citation, which look like duplicate or mis-tagged records. My attempt to open the database record returned HTTP 404. I have not read the paper, its abstract or any review.
events.delivers: Not established. The title indicates that the paper concerns square factors of Fermat numbers, which is the question itself, but I cannot determine whether it proves any result about p^2 dividing F_n, a restricted case, or a heuristic.
events.time_since_posted: About 46 years, if the 1980 date is right.
events.doubts: Cannot be assessed: no content read. The database records give conflicting journal names and years.

events.what_happened: Anders Björn and Hans Riesel, 'Factors of generalized Fermat numbers', Mathematics of Computation 67 (1998), pp. 441-446, DOI 10.1090/S0025-5718-98-00891-6. Per a search excerpt, its subject is a search for prime factors of generalized Fermat numbers a^(2^n) + b^(2^n). The Wikipedia Fermat number article, which I opened, cites it for an estimate of the number of square factors of Fermat numbers from F_5 onward, and concludes that there are unlikely to be any non-square-free Fermat numbers. I did not open the paper (the AMS page returned HTTP 403), so the estimate is as Wikipedia reports it. Two later errata concern the paper's factor tables, not the square-factor estimate as far as I can tell.
events.revisions: Table errata published 2005 and 2011 (per search excerpts, not opened).
events.delivers: A heuristic, not a result: an estimate of the expected number of square factors of Fermat numbers from F_5 on, which suggests that non-square-free Fermat numbers are unlikely. It proves nothing about any particular F_n.
events.doubts: Heuristic only, and the paper says so as Wikipedia reports it. I did not read the paper, so the estimate is unverified by me.

events.what_happened: On 16 December 2001 Jacques Basaldúa, on the PrimeNumbers mailing list and on his dybot.com page, claimed a proof that all Fermat and Mersenne numbers are square-free. The argument relies on the multiplicative order of 2 modulo odd integers and on the claim that the order of 2 modulo F_k is 2^(k+1). Pavlos N (message 4609 on the list) replied that the equation proved in section 4.2 is false and gave a counterexample at p = 1093, n = 2. He suggested the same obstacle affects Wieferich primes generally, and noted that the same technique had been tried on Mersenne numbers in 1996 with the same obstacle. The dybot.com page returned empty content when I fetched it, so I have the claim and the critique only as reported on the Prime Pages' Conjecture 12 page.
events.delivers: As claimed: a full resolution that no F_n has a square prime factor (and the same for Mersenne numbers). As critiqued: nothing established, since the step in section 4.2 is reported false.
events.remains: As claimed: nothing remains. As critiqued: the claim is not established, so the whole question remains open.

checked_by.what_they_did: Reported that the equation in section 4.2 is false, with a counterexample at p = 1093, n = 2
Pointed readers to his web page on the two known Wieferich primes; the record shows no engagement with the proof itself

events.doubts: The reported flaw is itself doubtful as written. The critique is reported as 'phi(p^n) = p^(n-1) phi(p) fails for p = 1093 and n = 2'. For n = 2 that identity reads phi(p^2) = p(p-1) = p*phi(p), which holds for every prime p, so it cannot be the failing step as stated. Either the Prime Pages summary of the critique is garbled, or the failing step is different. I did not see the proof text (dybot.com returned empty), so the claimed flaw is unresolved rather than confirmed. No reply from the author was found.
events.direction: Claims the full statement: no F_n has a square prime factor. Its validity is disputed in the critique.

events.what_happened: Jiří Klaška, 'Jakóbczyk's hypothesis on Mersenne numbers and generalizations of Skula's theorem', Journal of Integer Sequences 26 (2023), Article 23.3.8, pp. 1-21. Received 9 February 2023, published 17 March 2023. The abstract responds to Skula's result on prime-power divisors of Mersenne numbers, which it calls 'closely related to Jakóbczyk's hypothesis', and generalises it to a^n ± 1 for a >= 2. The keywords on the Brno record include 'Fermat number' and 'Wieferich prime'. The journal page's abstract does not mention Fermat numbers. A search excerpt says the paper also states the Fermat version of Jakóbczyk's hypothesis, namely that each Fermat number is a product of distinct odd primes; I could not confirm this, because the PDF did not decode.
events.delivers: On the Mersenne side of Jakóbczyk's hypothesis: a generalisation of Skula's divisibility result to a^n ± 1. On the Fermat side, as far as I could read: nothing confirmed.
events.remains: All of the Fermat question, as far as the readable material shows.
events.doubts: None active found. The Fermat-version claim rests only on a search excerpt I could not confirm.
events.direction: Not about the Fermat question as far as I could read. If it restates the Fermat version, it does so as a hypothesis; the readable abstract does not claim to prove it.

events.what_happened: Jiří Klaška, 'Fermat Numbers Modulo a Prime', Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.8.7. Received 18 June 2024, revised 29 April 2025, published 15 December 2025. The abstract analyses and refines Aigner's 1986 theorem on the periodicity of the sequence of Fermat numbers reduced modulo a prime, and says that Aigner's theorem 'can be substantially simplified and also refined'. The abstract does not mention square-freeness, Jakóbczyk's hypothesis or Wieferich primes. I did not read the full text.

events.delivers: Nothing on square-freeness. It concerns the residues of F_n modulo a fixed prime p (periodicity), not prime squares dividing F_n.

Search excerpts, which I did not open in full, describe it as: a short historical introduction; a focus on Jakóbczyk's 1951 hypothesis that all Fermat numbers are square-free; placement in the context of generalized Fermat-number sequences; Goldbach's 1730 result that distinct Fermat numbers are coprime; and a link between Hypothesis 1 and an unsolved Wieferich-prime problem. The same excerpts give an acceptance date of 25 May 2026. The PDF could not be decoded by any route I tried, so I cannot say what the notes establish.

events.what_happened: Erdős Problems forum, thread 1209 (Erdős Problem #1209: sequences n + a_k that are always prime or always squarefree, and whether n + 2^(2^k) can be always prime or always squarefree). User ebarschkis (15 April 2026) reported closing the three main questions after exploring ideas with GPT Pro, linked a TeX file, a PDF and a Lean formalisation, and guessed that 'the squarefree questions are at their core' the question whether all Fermat numbers are squarefree, which they called 'a famous open problem'. Nat Sothanaphan (16 April) ran a standard ChatGPT check that 'found no issues'. Thomas Bloom (17 April) noted that the first two variants were already answered by a trivial construction; ebarschkis then gave a stronger version with n = 0 as the unique shift. I read the thread through a summarising fetch, not verbatim; it states that the always-squarefree, infinitely-often-prime and infinitely-often-squarefree variants remain open.
events.revisions: Later posts on the thread: 16-17 April 2026, and 13 September 2026.
events.delivers: A neighbouring question only. The posted result concerns whether n + 2^(2^k) is always prime (answered: no n works), plus trivial constructions for the first two variants. None of it bears on whether any F_n is square-free. The Fermat link is one poster's guess.

events.what_happened: ProofAtlas (a 'Collaboration beta' page), 'Square-Freeness of Fermat Numbers', at proofatlas.ai/collaboration/fermat-numbers-are-square-free/. The page poses 'Can any prime square divide a Fermat number?' and says the question 'remains open'. It reports partial results, each labelled 'source-reported' and unaudited on the page: a retained necessary condition E > 7t; an exclusion of negative sixth carries for 7t < E <= 8t; an 'effective polynomial theorem' said to apply for E >= 2048, with finite completion through n = 10 relying on published F_9 and F_10 factor primality; and a 'negative seventh-band closure', which the page calls 'not a proof of square-freeness'. It says positive and higher-band cases remain open, and that a six-polynomial certificate 'was not executed or checked during this preparation'. The page names no author. It gives 'Source recorded' as 8 September 2026 and 'Status checked' as 20 August 2026, and says later revisions occurred without dates. I read it through a summarising fetch, so quotations are as that fetch returned them.
events.revisions: Revisions 'not established' per the page. The page's own dates are inconsistent: the status check (20 August 2026) precedes the source record (8 September 2026).
events.delivers: As the page describes it: partial exclusions for certain carry configurations in parameter bands, and a claimed effective result for E >= 2048 which, with factor data, would complete the square-freeness check through n = 10. The page says explicitly that this is not a proof of square-freeness for all n. The n <= 10 completion relies on factorisations that are already published, so it adds no new knowledge of individual F_n beyond the finite cases.
events.remains: Square-freeness for all n >= 11, and every band the page does not close (it says the positive and higher-band cases remain open).
events.doubts: The page labels every progress claim 'source-reported' and unaudited. The six-polynomial certificate was not executed or checked, by its own account. No named author, reviewer or formal artifact is given; the page lists 'formalization targets' as proposals only. It cites Warren and Bray (1967) and Wikipedia as its only checked sources. Its 'Source recorded' date is later than its 'Status checked' date. It excludes 'model runs' from counting as mathematical updates, which suggests machine-generated material in the project workflow, but names no system (see ai).
events.direction: Partial. It claims band-by-band progress and disclaims the full result; it does not assert the square-freeness claim or its negation.

events.what_happened: Nobuki Fujimoto, 'Paper 176 v0.1 - Fermat Numbers F_5-F_11: Empirical v_2(omega_{F_n}(3)) Measurement + Lean 4 Axiom-Free F_9 Excess Witness (Rei-AIOS)', posted on DEV Community (dev.to, 'Posted on Jul 29'; its status line gives 2026-07-30). The author lists 'Rei' and 'Claude' as co-architects. The paper measures the 2-adic valuation of the multiplicative order of 3 modulo prime factors of F_5 through F_11, and presents a Lean 4 witness that F_9 has excess at least 5 over Lucas's lower bound n + 2, with main factor 2424833. According to the summarising fetch, it does not discuss whether F_n is square-free or any square factor. I did not open the HackMD mirror.
events.revisions: v0.1 per the title. DEV shows 29 July; the paper's status line gives 30 July as the publish date.
events.delivers: Nothing on square-freeness. It gives multiplicative-order data for F_5 through F_11 and a claimed Lean bound for F_9, neither concerning prime squares dividing F_n.
events.doubts: Self-published v0.1, with AI co-authors credited and no peer review. The sorry-free and axiom-free status is the authors' own claim; I did not check the Lean files. Per the summarising fetch, some order computations were done in external Python rather than in Lean, and the authors' own axiom audit shows dependence on Mathlib's standard axioms.

disputes.summary: The 2001 Basaldúa claimed proof that all Fermat and Mersenne numbers are square-free: Pavlos N reports a false step (section 4.2) with a counterexample. The reported counterexample is doubtful as written, because the identity quoted, phi(p^n) = p^(n-1) phi(p), holds for every prime p. The proof text was not readable to me, so the dispute is unresolved; no author reply was found.

Neighbouring question, Erdős Problem #1209 (not Fermat numbers): a 13 September 2026 post says the problem was used in an ELMO competition, proposed by Jack Gurev, with a solution given in 2015; a reply says GPT is 'not the best at attribution'. Recorded because it concerns AI credit in the same thread; unresolved.

summary: I ran 36 searches (listed below) covering the problem's name and variants, the 1967 criterion, Jakóbczyk and Klaška's papers, factorisation progress, Wieferich-prime searches, the sister problem for Euclid numbers, and AI sources (lab papers, AI-Erdős trackers and forum threads, Lean repositories, Quanta). I opened the primary sources I could reach. Nothing found settles the question or a substantial case of it. The oldest substantive item is Warren and Bray (1967), Pacific J. Math. 22(3): if any F_n were not square-free, its square prime factor p would satisfy 2^(p-1) = 1 (mod p^2), and neither of the two then-known Wieferich primes divides a Fermat or Mersenne number. I read its abstract only, because the PDF would not decode. Ribenboim (1980) on square factors of Fermat numbers is a database record only (the record page returned 404), so its content is unknown. Björn and Riesel (1998) give a heuristic, as Wikipedia reports it, that non-square-free Fermat numbers are unlikely; the paper's AMS page returned 403. Basaldúa (2001) claimed a full proof; the critique reported by Prime Pages says a step fails at p = 1093, n = 2, but the identity quoted holds for every prime, so the critique as reported is doubtful, and the dybot.com page came back empty. Since 26 January 2024 the Fermat-specific events are: (a) Klaška, 'Several Notes on Jakóbczyk's Hypothesis on Fermat Numbers', Integers 26 (2026) #A77, published and deposited 26 June 2026 (Zenodo DOI 10.5281/zenodo.20931052). The index page and Zenodo record are opened, but the PDF would not decode by any route, so I cannot say what the notes establish. Search excerpts describe a restatement of Hypothesis 1 linked to a Wieferich problem, with no proof of the hypothesis or a case of it reported in them. (b) ProofAtlas's 'Square-Freeness of Fermat Numbers' page (2026, no named author) reports band-by-band partial progress and says outright that it is not a proof of square-freeness. (c) Seven FermatSearch factor announcements (May 2024 to December 2025) add new prime divisors of composite F_n; they bear on the factorisation record, not on square factors. Klaška's 2025 JIS paper concerns Aigner's periodicity mod p, and the 2023 JIS paper concerns Mersenne numbers, with a Fermat version I could not confirm. The Erdős #1209 thread (April 2026) credits GPT Pro with closing neighbouring questions; the squarefree variants there remain open, and the link to Fermat squarefreeness is one poster's guess. The Fujimoto 'Paper 176' (29-30 July 2026) credits Claude (claude-opus-4-7) and Rei as co-architects, but it measures multiplicative orders of 3 modulo prime factors of F_5 to F_11 and does not discuss square factors. No AI system is credited with a step toward this question. Close calls: the 2026 Integers note might contain a partial result I could not read, and the ProofAtlas band results might be counted as a case by a later pass, though the page disclaims them. The Wikipedia Fermat number article lists this as open; the text I read is undated, and a search summary dated it December 2025. Manifold's market (91% at the time of reading) is sentiment, not evidence. A February 2026 Caldwell note on Mersenne numbers gives the Wieferich search limit as 2^64 with only 1093 and 3511 below it; that limit bears on the 1967 criterion but is not a Fermat result.
competing_reading: The strongest reading is that the question is nearly settled in practice: a search summary of Wikipedia says complete factorisations are known for F_0 to F_11, and Manifold's note says every Fermat number whose factorisation is known is square-free, so the finite cases are covered; the 1967 criterion (with the Wieferich search to 2^64) narrows any counterexample to a Wieferich prime beyond the search range; and the Björn and Riesel heuristic says counterexamples are unlikely. On that reading the problem is open but strongly supported. The opposing reading is that none of this is a proof, the finite cases do not reach any n beyond the known factorisations, the 1967 criterion excludes only Wieferich primes that are checked, and the 2001 proof's critique is itself doubtful. The Klaška 2026 note could also be read as a partial result that the search excerpts omit.
what_would_settle_it: The full text of Klaška's Integers A77 (the exact statement of Hypothesis 1, and whether any note proves a partial case), read from a working PDF or the journal's own page; the 1967 Warren and Bray PDF; the 1980 Ribenboim paper; the 1998 Björn and Riesel paper, to check the square-factor heuristic; the dybot.com proof and any author reply, to see whether the step criticised is the one the proof uses; the identity and credentials of the ProofAtlas authors, and an independent check of its finite-completion claim; a primary table of complete factorisations of F_0 to F_11 with a square-freeness statement for each; and a systematic arXiv search for 2026 Fermat square-free papers, which this search tool could not run directly.

judgement.why: No event settles, restricts or bounds the question 'are all Fermat numbers square-free?'. Warren-Bray 1967 is a reduction to the Wieferich condition (none). Björn-Riesel is a heuristic (none). New prime factors of composite F_n, Klaška's Mersenne and mod-p papers, the Erdős #1209 variants and Fujimoto's order computations are different questions (variant). Klaška 2026, as far as anything readable shows, restates the hypothesis as open (none). The close call was ProofAtlas. Its band exclusions are not restrictions to a class of n. Its finite completion to n<=10 is instances already known from factorisations, and the page disclaims any proof, so it is none and doubtful. Basaldúa's 2001 claim is set aside as not credible: it is an old mailing-list proof of a famous problem, it drew an unanswered critique, it was taken up by no one, and later literature still calls the problem open. The AI credits do not count. Fujimoto's 'Co-architect' label says nothing about what Claude or Rei produced, and in any case the paper is off-question. The Erdős thread has no systems entry. Both are none.
